questions.q: What is the largest animal alive today?
questions.fact: Blue whales can grow to about 30 metres long, longer than two buses.

questions.q: Which is the fastest land animal?
questions.fact: A cheetah can sprint at around 100 km/h, but only in short bursts.

questions.q: Which animal is the tallest in the world?
questions.fact: A giraffe's long neck has seven bones, the same number as a human neck.

questions.q: How many legs does a spider have?
questions.fact: Spiders are arachnids, not insects. Insects have six legs.

questions.q: What do bees make from flower nectar?
questions.fact: Honeybees store honey as food for the colony to eat through the winter.

questions.q: What is a baby kangaroo called?
questions.fact: A newborn joey is about the size of a jelly bean and grows in its mother's pouch.

questions.q: Which of these birds cannot fly?
questions.fact: Penguins use their wings as flippers and are excellent swimmers.

questions.q: Which of these mammals can truly fly?
questions.fact: Bats are the only mammals capable of true flight; flying squirrels can only glide.

questions.q: What does a caterpillar grow up to become?
questions.fact: The change happens inside a chrysalis or cocoon and is called metamorphosis.

questions.q: What do giant pandas mainly eat?
questions.fact: Giant pandas spend about half of each day eating bamboo.

questions.q: How many hearts does an octopus have?
questions.fact: Two hearts pump blood to the gills and one pumps it around the rest of the body.

questions.q: What does a camel store in its hump?
questions.fact: The fat in a camel's hump is an energy store that helps it travel far without food.

questions.q: What is a group of lions called?
questions.fact: Lions are the most social of all the big cats.

questions.q: Which reptile is famous for changing its skin colour?
questions.fact: Chameleons change colour mainly to signal their mood and to control their temperature.

questions.q: A frog starts its life as a...
questions.fact: Tadpoles breathe through gills and grow legs as they turn into frogs.

questions.q: Dolphins belong to which group of animals?
questions.fact: Dolphins breathe air through a blowhole and feed their young with milk.

questions.q: Which is the largest bird in the world?
questions.fact: An ostrich egg is the largest of any living bird and weighs over a kilogram.

questions.q: What is the process plants use to make food from sunlight?
questions.fact: During photosynthesis plants take in carbon dioxide and give out oxygen.

questions.q: Which bird can fly backwards?
questions.fact: Hummingbirds beat their wings so fast that they can hover in one spot.

questions.q: Koalas mainly eat the leaves of which tree?
questions.fact: Eucalyptus leaves give little energy, so koalas sleep for most of the day.

questions.q: What is a group of crows called?
questions.fact: Many animal group names are old hunting terms, like a parliament of owls.

questions.q: Bamboo is a type of...
questions.fact: Some kinds of bamboo can grow almost a metre in a single day.

questions.q: Which animal has fingerprints very like a human's?
questions.fact: Koala fingerprints are so similar to ours that they are hard to tell apart.

questions.q: What is the green pigment in plants called?
questions.fact: Chlorophyll absorbs red and blue light and reflects green, so leaves look green.

questions.q: What is a shark's skeleton made of?
questions.fact: Cartilage is the same flexible material found in your nose and ears.

questions.q: How many legs does an insect have?
questions.fact: An insect's six legs all grow from its thorax, the middle part of its three-part body.

questions.q: Which is the heaviest living land animal?
questions.fact: An adult male African bush elephant weighs about 6 tonnes on average, about as much as four cars.

questions.q: What is an animal that eats both plants and meat called?
questions.fact: Brown bears are omnivores: they eat berries, roots and grass as well as fish and small mammals.

questions.q: Which of these mammals lays eggs?
questions.fact: The platypus and the echidnas are the only egg-laying mammals, yet their young still feed on milk.

questions.q: The kiwi, a flightless bird, is native to which country?
questions.fact: Kiwis are the only birds with nostrils at the tip of the beak, which they use to sniff out worms.

questions.q: Lemurs are native to which island?
questions.fact: Lemurs are primates, like monkeys and apes. Ring-tailed lemurs often hold their striped tails up high, like flags, as they move.

questions.q: Which slow-moving rainforest animal spends most of its life hanging upside down?
questions.fact: Tiny green algae grow in a sloth's shaggy fur, giving it a greenish tint that helps it hide among leaves.

questions.q: Which animal builds dams across streams using sticks and mud?
questions.fact: A beaver's front teeth never stop growing, and they are orange because their enamel contains iron.

questions.q: How many arms do most starfish have?
questions.fact: Starfish have no brain and no blood, and many can regrow an arm they have lost.

questions.q: Clownfish live safely among the stinging tentacles of which animal?
questions.fact: Slimy mucus on its skin stops the anemone stinging it, and in return the fish chases off anemone-eating fish.

questions.q: Which insects build tall mounds of earth in Africa and Australia?
questions.fact: Some termite mounds stand taller than a person, built grain by grain from soil, saliva and droppings.

questions.q: What mainly carries dandelion seeds to new places?
questions.fact: Each dandelion seed hangs beneath a tiny parachute of fine hairs called a pappus.

questions.q: What can you work out by counting the rings in a tree trunk?
questions.fact: In places with seasons, a tree usually adds one ring a year: a pale band in spring and a darker one later.

questions.q: Mushrooms belong to which group of living things?
questions.fact: A mushroom is just the fruiting part of a fungus; most of it is a web of threads hidden in soil or wood.

questions.q: What do many bats use to hunt insects in the dark?
questions.fact: Bats make high-pitched calls and listen for the echoes. Most of these calls are too high for people to hear.

questions.q: Where do female sea turtles lay their eggs?
questions.fact: Many females return to nest near the beach where they hatched, often decades later.

questions.q: Which long-haired relative of cattle lives high on the Tibetan Plateau?
questions.fact: Wild yaks have such thick, shaggy coats that they can cope with temperatures as low as −40 °C.

questions.q: Which spiny mammal rolls itself into a tight ball when it feels threatened?
questions.fact: A hedgehog has thousands of spines, each one a stiff, hollow hair made of keratin.

questions.q: Which fish swims back up the river where it hatched to lay its eggs?
questions.fact: Salmon find their home river partly by smell, remembering its scent from when they were young.

questions.q: Which bird of India is famous for the male's huge fan of eye-spotted feathers?
questions.fact: The fan, called a train, is not really a tail: it grows from feathers above the tail and is shed each year.

questions.q: Which animal's name comes from Greek words meaning 'river horse'?
questions.fact: Hippos make their own sunscreen: a reddish fluid, neither blood nor sweat, that oozes from their skin.

questions.q: The okapi of Central Africa is most closely related to which animal?
questions.fact: Despite its zebra-like striped legs, the okapi is in the giraffe family and has a long, grasping tongue.

questions.q: Which is the largest living rodent?
questions.fact: Capybaras live near rivers and lakes in South America, and their slightly webbed feet make them good swimmers.

questions.q: Which is the largest living fish?
questions.fact: Despite its size, the whale shark is a gentle filter feeder that eats plankton and small fish.

questions.q: In seahorses, which parent carries the eggs until the young are born?
questions.fact: The female puts her eggs into a pouch on the male's belly, and weeks later he gives birth to the young.

questions.q: Which penguin father keeps the egg warm on his feet through the Antarctic winter?
questions.fact: The males huddle together against the cold and go without food for months while the females feed at sea.

questions.q: Fireflies are actually a type of which insect?
questions.fact: Fireflies make light through a chemical reaction in their bodies that gives off almost no heat.

questions.q: About how far can an owl turn its head?
questions.fact: Owls must turn their heads because their tube-shaped eyes cannot move in their sockets.

questions.q: What colour is a polar bear's skin?
questions.fact: Its fur isn't truly white either: each hair is see-through and only looks white because it scatters light.

questions.q: Which Australian animal is famous for its cube-shaped droppings?
questions.fact: The cubes take shape inside the wombat's gut, where some parts of the wall are stiffer than others.

questions.q: North America's eastern monarch butterflies spend the winter in which country?
questions.fact: No single butterfly makes the whole round trip: the journey back north takes several generations.

questions.q: Which seabird flies each year from the far north to the edge of Antarctica and back?
questions.fact: Over its life, an Arctic tern may fly a distance equal to about three trips to the Moon and back.

questions.q: Corals look like plants or rocks, but what are they really?
questions.fact: Tiny algae living inside coral tissue make food from sunlight and give many corals their colours.

questions.q: Which African tree stores huge amounts of water in its swollen trunk?
questions.fact: Baobabs can live for well over 1,000 years, and their fruit is rich in vitamin C.

questions.q: Which Indian tree sends down roots from its branches that grow into new trunks?
questions.fact: The banyan is a kind of fig. An old one can spread so wide that it looks like a small forest.

questions.q: The Sundarbans, a vast delta forest famous for its tigers, is made up mainly of which kind of tree?
questions.fact: Mangrove roots poke up out of the mud like snorkels, helping the trees breathe in waterlogged soil.

questions.q: Which is the longest venomous snake?
questions.fact: King cobras live in the forests of India and Southeast Asia and feed mostly on other snakes.

questions.q: Wild orangutans live only on Borneo and which other island?
questions.fact: Their name comes from Malay words meaning 'person of the forest', and they spend most of their lives in trees.

questions.q: What does a honeybee's 'waggle dance' tell other bees?
questions.fact: The angle of the waggle shows the direction compared with the Sun, and how long it lasts shows the distance.

questions.q: Which bird is famous for laying its eggs in other birds' nests?
questions.fact: The foster parents raise the cuckoo chick as their own, even when it grows much bigger than them.

questions.q: Which insect was the first shown to use the Milky Way to keep its bearings at night?
questions.fact: On moonless nights, these beetles use the glow of the Milky Way to roll their dung balls in a straight line.

questions.q: Which of these animals is one of the elephant's closest living relatives?
questions.fact: Elephants, sea cows (manatees and dugongs) and small, furry hyraxes form one closely related group of mammals.

questions.q: Which New Zealand parrot cannot fly?
questions.fact: The kakapo is the world's heaviest parrot. It is active at night and climbs trees instead of flying.

questions.q: Vanilla flavouring comes from the pods of which kind of plant?
questions.fact: Vanilla orchids come from Mexico and Central America. Elsewhere, growers must pollinate each flower by hand.

questions.q: The Venus flytrap is native to which country?
questions.fact: Its trap snaps shut only if trigger hairs are touched twice in quick succession, so raindrops rarely set it off.

questions.q: Which tiny animal is nicknamed the 'water bear'?
questions.fact: Tardigrades can survive drying out completely by curling up into a dormant state called a tun.

questions.q: Which fish, known only from fossils, was found alive off South Africa in 1938?
questions.fact: Scientists had thought coelacanths died out with the dinosaurs, around 66 million years ago.

questions.q: Saffron, the costly spice, comes from which flower?
questions.fact: Each flower gives just three red threads, so it takes well over 100,000 flowers to make one kilogram.

questions.q: In sea turtles, what decides whether an egg hatches as a male or a female?
questions.fact: Warmer sand produces mostly females and cooler sand mostly males.

questions.q: Which South American bird's chicks have claws on their wings to help them climb?
questions.fact: The hoatzin digests leaves by fermenting them, a bit like a cow, which gives it a strong farmyard smell.

questions.q: What is the capital of France?
questions.fact: The Eiffel Tower in Paris was built for the 1889 World's Fair.

questions.q: What is the largest ocean on Earth?
questions.fact: The Pacific Ocean covers more area than all of Earth's land put together.

questions.q: Which is the largest continent by area?
questions.fact: Asia is home to about six in every ten people on Earth.

questions.q: What is the highest mountain above sea level?
questions.fact: Mount Everest stands on the border between Nepal and China.

questions.q: Which country is shaped like a boot?
questions.fact: The toe of the Italian boot points towards the island of Sicily.

questions.q: The Sahara Desert is on which continent?
questions.fact: The Sahara is the largest hot desert in the world.

questions.q: What is the capital of Japan?
questions.fact: Kyoto was Japan's capital for more than a thousand years before Tokyo.

questions.q: Which line divides Earth into the Northern and Southern Hemispheres?
questions.fact: The equator is about 40,000 km long.

questions.q: How many continents are usually counted on Earth?
questions.fact: They are Africa, Antarctica, Asia, Australia, Europe, North America and South America.

questions.q: Which river flows through Cairo in Egypt?
questions.fact: The Nile flows north and empties into the Mediterranean Sea.

questions.q: What is the capital of India?
questions.fact: Until 1911 the capital of British India was Calcutta, the city known today as Kolkata.

questions.q: Off the coast of which country is the Great Barrier Reef?
questions.fact: The Great Barrier Reef is the largest coral reef system in the world.

questions.q: What is the capital of Australia?
questions.fact: Canberra was purpose-built as a compromise between rivals Sydney and Melbourne.

questions.q: What is the capital of Canada?
questions.fact: Queen Victoria chose Ottawa as the capital in 1857.

questions.q: What is the capital of Brazil?
questions.fact: Brasília was built from scratch and became the capital in 1960.

questions.q: What is the capital of Turkey?
questions.fact: Istanbul is Turkey's biggest city, but Ankara has been the capital since 1923.

questions.q: Mount Kilimanjaro is in which country?
questions.fact: Kilimanjaro is the highest mountain in Africa, at about 5,895 metres.

questions.q: Which is the largest country in the world by area?
questions.fact: Russia stretches across 11 time zones.

questions.q: Which is the largest island in the world, not counting Australia?
questions.fact: Greenland is part of the Kingdom of Denmark, and most of it is covered by ice.

questions.q: Which strait separates Spain from Morocco?
questions.fact: At its narrowest, the Strait of Gibraltar is only about 14 km wide.

questions.q: The Prime Meridian runs through Greenwich, in which city?
questions.fact: Time zones around the world are measured from the Prime Meridian at 0° longitude.

questions.q: Which US state is made up entirely of islands?
questions.fact: Hawaii's islands were formed by volcanoes, and some of them are still active.

questions.q: Which river flows through London?
questions.fact: The Thames flows east through London on its way to the North Sea.

questions.q: What is the capital of Egypt?
questions.fact: The pyramids of Giza stand on the edge of greater Cairo.

questions.q: What is the capital of New Zealand?
questions.fact: Wellington is often called the southernmost capital city of a sovereign state.

questions.q: What is the capital of Nigeria?
questions.fact: Abuja replaced Lagos as Nigeria's capital in 1991.

questions.q: What is the capital of Morocco?
questions.fact: Casablanca is Morocco's biggest city, but the capital is Rabat.

questions.q: Into which sea does the River Danube flow?
questions.fact: The Danube flows through more countries than any other river in the world.

questions.q: In which ocean trench is the deepest known point on Earth?
questions.fact: The Challenger Deep in the Mariana Trench is nearly 11 km below sea level.

questions.q: What is the capital of Vietnam?
questions.fact: Ho Chi Minh City, once called Saigon, is Vietnam's largest city.

questions.q: Which country's flag is white with a red circle in the centre?
questions.fact: Japanese people often call the flag Hinomaru, which means 'circle of the sun'.

questions.q: Mount Everest sits on the border between China and which country?
questions.fact: Its Nepali name is Sagarmatha, and its Tibetan name is Chomolungma.

questions.q: What is the capital of China?
questions.fact: Beijing was the first city to host both the Summer and the Winter Olympic Games.

questions.q: Which mountain range lies along India's northern border?
questions.fact: The name Himalaya comes from Sanskrit and means 'abode of snow'.

questions.q: Which is the coldest continent on Earth?
questions.fact: About 98% of it is covered in ice, yet it is also the driest and windiest continent.

questions.q: Which is the smallest of the world's oceans?
questions.fact: It is also the shallowest ocean, and it surrounds the North Pole.

questions.q: Into which ocean does the Amazon River flow?
questions.fact: It carries more water than any other river, about a fifth of all river water reaching the oceans.

questions.q: Which mountain range runs down the western side of South America?
questions.fact: They are the longest mountain range on land, running through seven countries.

questions.q: Which famous waterfalls lie on the border between Canada and the USA?
questions.fact: They are made up of three falls: Horseshoe Falls, American Falls and Bridal Veil Falls.

questions.q: In which city does the Statue of Liberty stand?
questions.fact: It stands on Liberty Island, and its copper skin slowly turned from shiny brown to green as it weathered.

questions.q: In which Italian city is the famous Leaning Tower?
questions.fact: It began to tilt in 1178, while still being built, because the ground beneath it is soft.

questions.q: Which country is famous for its long, deep sea inlets called fjords?
questions.fact: Fjords are valleys carved by glaciers and flooded by the sea; Norway's Sognefjord is over 200 km long.

questions.q: What is the capital of Madagascar?
questions.fact: Antananarivo sits in the island's central highlands, about 1,280 m above sea level.

questions.q: Which sea lies between southern Europe and northern Africa?
questions.fact: Its name comes from Latin words meaning 'in the middle of the land'.

questions.q: Which country is made up mainly of the North Island and the South Island?
questions.fact: The two islands are separated by Cook Strait, about 22 km wide at its narrowest point.

questions.q: What is a book of maps called?
questions.fact: The first modern atlas, made by Abraham Ortelius in 1570, was called 'Theatre of the World'.

questions.q: What do we call land almost surrounded by water but joined to the mainland?
questions.fact: The word comes from the Latin 'paene insula', meaning 'almost an island'.

questions.q: Which ocean lies between Africa and Australia?
questions.fact: It is the only ocean named after a country, and the Arabian Sea and Bay of Bengal are parts of it.

questions.q: Which line of latitude passes through the middle of India?
questions.fact: It crosses eight Indian states, from Gujarat in the west to Mizoram in the east.

questions.q: Which Indian city is known as the 'Pink City'?
questions.fact: In 1876 its old city was painted pink, a colour of hospitality, to welcome Britain's Prince of Wales.

questions.q: The Sundarbans delta forest is shared by India and which country?
questions.fact: Its Bengal tigers are strong swimmers that cross the channels between its many islands.

questions.q: The shores of which salty lake are the lowest dry land on Earth?
questions.fact: It is almost ten times saltier than the ocean, so swimmers float on it with ease.

questions.q: Which is the deepest lake in the world?
questions.fact: This Siberian lake is more than 1,600 m deep and holds about 20% of Earth's unfrozen fresh surface water.

questions.q: Which river is China's Three Gorges Dam built across?
questions.fact: The Yangtze is the longest river in Asia, and it flows entirely within China.

questions.q: How many time zones does China officially use?
questions.fact: China spans about five geographical time zones, but the whole country runs on Beijing Time.

questions.q: Victoria Falls is on which African river?
questions.fact: Its local name, Mosi-oa-Tunya, means 'the smoke that thunders', after its roaring spray.

questions.q: Which desert covers most of Botswana?
questions.fact: The Okavango River flows into the Kalahari and fans out into a vast inland delta instead of reaching the sea.

questions.q: The Suez Canal links the Mediterranean Sea with which other sea?
questions.fact: Opened in 1869, it has no locks, because the two seas are at nearly the same level.

questions.q: Which South American country is named after the equator?
questions.fact: Ecuador is Spanish for 'equator', and the line passes just north of the capital, Quito.

questions.q: Which desert in northern Chile is one of the driest places on Earth?
questions.fact: Its rocky, Mars-like landscape is used to test rovers and instruments built for Mars.

questions.q: Lake Titicaca lies on the border between Peru and which country?
questions.fact: At about 3,800 m above sea level, it is often called the highest navigable lake in the world.

questions.q: Which river carved the Grand Canyon?
questions.fact: The canyon is 446 km long and more than 1.8 km deep in places, exposing rocks almost 2 billion years old.

questions.q: Which island country lies on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, where tectonic plates pull apart?
questions.fact: At Thingvellir you can walk through the rift valley between the North American and Eurasian plates.

questions.q: Which Australian state is an island to the south of the mainland?
questions.fact: It is named after Dutch explorer Abel Tasman, the first European known to sight it, in 1642.

questions.q: Which country's flag has a navy blue wheel with 24 spokes at its centre?
questions.fact: The wheel, called the Ashoka Chakra, sits on a white band between saffron and green stripes.

questions.q: On a map, what are lines joining places of equal height called?
questions.fact: Where contour lines are close together the land is steep; where they are far apart it is gentle.

questions.q: Which Pacific country straddles both the equator and the 180° line of longitude?
questions.fact: Its Line Islands use UTC+14, so they are among the first places on Earth to start each new day.

questions.q: The summit of which mountain is the farthest point from Earth's centre?
questions.fact: Earth bulges at the equator, so this Ecuadorian volcano's summit is about 2 km farther out than Everest's.

questions.q: Which country is completely surrounded by South Africa?
questions.fact: Nicknamed the 'Kingdom in the Sky', it is the only country that lies entirely above 1,000 m.

questions.q: Which major African river crosses the equator twice?
questions.fact: The Congo is also the deepest river known, with depths of more than 200 metres.

questions.q: Which major Indian river flows west into the Arabian Sea?
questions.fact: It runs through a rift valley between the Vindhya and Satpura ranges, reaching the sea in Gujarat.

questions.q: Which map projection, made in 1569, makes Greenland look about as big as Africa?
questions.fact: It was designed to help sailors navigate, but in reality Africa is about 14 times larger than Greenland.

questions.q: Which sea has no land borders and is surrounded only by ocean currents?
questions.fact: It is named after floating sargassum seaweed, and European and American eels are thought to breed there.

questions.q: What is the capital of Mongolia?
questions.fact: Often called the world's coldest capital city, it can see winter temperatures below −30 °C.

questions.q: Into which body of water does the Volga, Europe's longest river, flow?
questions.fact: The Caspian has no outlet to the ocean, so it loses water mainly through evaporation.

questions.q: What is the chemical formula for water?
questions.fact: Each water molecule has two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom.

questions.q: At what temperature does water boil at sea level?
questions.fact: High on a mountain, water boils at a lower temperature because the air pressure is lower.

questions.q: Which gas do plants take in from the air to make food?
questions.fact: Plants give out oxygen as a by-product of making their food.

questions.q: What is the hardest natural substance?
questions.fact: Diamonds are made of carbon, the same element as the graphite in pencils.

questions.q: Which organ pumps blood around the body?
questions.fact: An adult heart beats about 100,000 times a day.

questions.q: What is the largest organ of the human body?
questions.fact: Your skin renews itself all the time, shedding millions of dead cells every day.

questions.q: Which force pulls objects towards the ground?
questions.fact: Isaac Newton described gravity in his book 'Principia' in 1687.

questions.q: At what temperature does water freeze?
questions.fact: On the Fahrenheit scale, water freezes at 32 degrees.

questions.q: How many bones are in an adult human body?
questions.fact: Babies are born with about 300 bones; some of them fuse together as they grow.

questions.q: Which gas do we need to breathe in to stay alive?
questions.fact: About one fifth of the air we breathe is oxygen.

questions.q: What is the chemical symbol for gold?
questions.fact: Au comes from 'aurum', the Latin word for gold.

questions.q: Which gas makes up most of Earth's air?
questions.fact: Nitrogen makes up about 78% of the air.

questions.q: Which metal is liquid at room temperature?
questions.fact: Mercury was once used in thermometers because it expands evenly when heated.

questions.q: What is the lightest chemical element?
questions.fact: Hydrogen is the most common element in the universe.

questions.q: How many chambers does the human heart have?
questions.fact: The two upper chambers are called atria and the two lower ones ventricles.

questions.q: Which scientist developed the theory of relativity?
questions.fact: Einstein's equation E = mc² shows that mass and energy are linked.

questions.q: Who discovered penicillin?
questions.fact: In 1928 Fleming noticed that a mould had killed the bacteria growing in a dish.

questions.q: Which vitamin does your skin make in sunlight?
questions.fact: Vitamin D helps the body absorb calcium for strong bones.

questions.q: What is the pH of pure water?
questions.fact: A pH below 7 is acidic and above 7 is alkaline.

questions.q: Sound travels fastest through which of these?
questions.fact: Sound travels more than 15 times faster through steel than through air.

questions.q: What is the chemical symbol for sodium?
questions.fact: Na comes from 'natrium', the Latin name for sodium.

questions.q: What is the SI unit of force?
questions.fact: One newton is roughly the weight of a small apple.

questions.q: Which blood type is known as the universal donor?
questions.fact: AB positive is called the universal recipient: it can receive red cells from any type.

questions.q: Which part of a cell holds most of its DNA?
questions.fact: Uncoiled, the DNA in a single human cell would stretch about 2 metres.

questions.q: Roughly how fast does light travel in a vacuum?
questions.fact: Light from the Sun takes about 8 minutes to reach Earth.

questions.q: Which gas is used to fill party balloons so that they float?
questions.fact: Helium is the second lightest element, and unlike hydrogen it does not burn, which makes it safe to use.

questions.q: Which organ controls your body by sending signals along nerves?
questions.fact: The human brain has around 86 billion nerve cells, called neurons, linked by trillions of connections.

questions.q: What is it called when a gas cools and turns into a liquid?
questions.fact: Droplets form on a cold drink because water vapour in the air cools and condenses on the glass.

questions.q: How many colours are traditionally named in a rainbow?
questions.fact: Isaac Newton settled on seven colours, partly to match the seven notes of a musical scale.

questions.q: Which of these particles has a negative charge?
questions.fact: An electron has about 1/1836 of a proton's mass, so almost all of an atom's mass is in its nucleus.

questions.q: Which of these metals is strongly attracted to a magnet?
questions.fact: Iron, nickel and cobalt are the common metals that magnets attract strongly, and steel is mostly iron.

questions.q: Oranges and lemons are rich in which vitamin?
questions.fact: Unlike most mammals, humans cannot make their own vitamin C, so we must get it from food.

questions.q: Which part of the body filters your blood to make urine?
questions.fact: Your kidneys filter about 180 litres of fluid from your blood each day, and put almost all of it back.

questions.q: Which force resists motion when two surfaces rub together?
questions.fact: Without friction you could not walk: your shoes would slip on the ground with every step.

questions.q: Roughly what is normal human body temperature?
questions.fact: Body temperature is usually a little lower in the early morning and a little higher in the late afternoon.

questions.q: Which unit is used to measure how loud a sound is?
questions.fact: The decibel scale is logarithmic: each rise of 10 decibels means ten times as much sound energy.

questions.q: Sound cannot travel through which of these?
questions.fact: Sound is a vibration passed from particle to particle, so where there are no particles there is no sound.

questions.q: Which of these is a renewable source of energy?
questions.fact: Winds are driven by the Sun heating Earth unevenly, so wind power is really a form of solar energy.

questions.q: What is the smallest unit of life?
questions.fact: Bacteria are made of just one cell, while an adult human body has tens of trillions of them.

questions.q: Your bones and teeth hold almost all of your body's supply of which mineral?
questions.fact: Bone is living tissue that is constantly rebuilt, and it releases calcium into the blood whenever the body needs more.

questions.q: What type of energy does an object have because it is moving?
questions.fact: Kinetic energy grows with the square of speed, so going twice as fast means four times the energy.

questions.q: Newton's third law says every action has an equal and opposite what?
questions.fact: Rockets rely on it: they push hot gas out backwards, and the gas pushes the rocket forwards.

questions.q: Which of these is acidic?
questions.fact: Lemon juice has a pH of about 2, mainly because of the citric acid it contains.

questions.q: Which organ in the human body makes bile?
questions.fact: The liver can grow back to its full size even after a large part of it has been removed.

questions.q: What gives red blood cells their red colour?
questions.fact: Haemoglobin contains iron, and it turns bright red when it picks up oxygen in the lungs.

questions.q: What is the longest bone in the human body?
questions.fact: The femur, or thigh bone, is roughly a quarter of a person's height.

questions.q: How many pairs of chromosomes are in a typical human body cell?
questions.fact: One chromosome of each pair comes from each parent, giving 46 in all.

questions.q: What is the hardest substance in the human body?
questions.fact: Enamel is about 96% mineral and has no living cells, so the body cannot regrow it once it is lost.

questions.q: What is the chemical symbol for silver?
questions.fact: Ag comes from argentum, the Latin word for silver, which also gave Argentina its name.

questions.q: Which gas has the chemical formula CH₄?
questions.fact: Methane is the main part of natural gas, and cows release a lot of it as they digest grass.

questions.q: What do we call a substance that speeds up a reaction without being used up?
questions.fact: Enzymes are catalysts made by living things; in your gut they help break down the food you eat.

questions.q: Bronze is mainly copper mixed with which other metal?
questions.fact: Brass is a different alloy, of copper and zinc. Bronze mattered so much that it gave its name to the Bronze Age.

questions.q: Roughly how fast does sound travel through air?
questions.fact: Thunder lags behind lightning because sound takes about 3 seconds to travel 1 kilometre.

questions.q: What is the SI unit of energy?
questions.fact: One joule is roughly the energy needed to lift a small apple one metre.

questions.q: Roughly what is absolute zero, the coldest possible temperature?
questions.fact: Absolute zero is 0 kelvin, the point at which particles have the least energy they possibly can.

questions.q: Which colour of visible light has the longest wavelength?
questions.fact: Just beyond red lies infrared light, which we cannot see but can feel as warmth.

questions.q: Which part of the eye contains the cells that detect light?
questions.fact: The retina has rods, which work in dim light, and cones, which let us see colour.

questions.q: Which element did Marie and Pierre Curie name after Poland?
questions.fact: The Curies announced polonium in July 1898, a few months before they announced radium.

questions.q: Which chemist's periodic table predicted elements that had not yet been found?
questions.fact: Elements he predicted, such as gallium and germanium, were discovered within 20 years.

questions.q: Which scientist discovered the basic rules of heredity by breeding pea plants?
questions.fact: Mendel's work was largely overlooked until 1900, 16 years after his death.

questions.q: Which physicist discovered X-rays in 1895?
questions.fact: Röntgen won the first Nobel Prize in Physics, in 1901, and chose not to patent his discovery.

questions.q: What is the smallest bone in the human body?
questions.fact: The stapes sits in the middle ear, is about 3 mm long and is shaped like a stirrup.

questions.q: Which Indian physicist won a Nobel Prize for his discovery about how light scatters?
questions.fact: India celebrates National Science Day each year on 28 February to mark Raman's discovery in 1928.

questions.q: Who wrote the 'Book of Optics', explaining that we see when light enters our eyes?
questions.fact: Working in Cairo about 1,000 years ago, Ibn al-Haytham tested his ideas with careful experiments.

questions.q: Chinese scientist Tu Youyou won a Nobel Prize for a new treatment for which disease?
questions.fact: She found the drug artemisinin in sweet wormwood, a herb used in traditional Chinese medicine.

questions.q: Which element makes up the largest share of the human body by mass?
questions.fact: Hydrogen atoms are the most numerous, but oxygen atoms are about 16 times heavier, so oxygen wins by mass.

questions.q: Which element has the chemical symbol K?
questions.fact: K comes from kalium, a name rooted in the Arabic for plant ashes, which also gave us the word 'alkali'.

questions.q: At what temperature do the Celsius and Fahrenheit scales give the same reading?
questions.fact: Setting F = 1.8 × C + 32 equal to C gives −40, the only temperature where the two scales agree.

questions.q: Which physicist discovered the electron in 1897?
questions.fact: Thomson pictured the atom as a 'plum pudding', with electrons dotted through a ball of positive charge.

questions.q: Which vitamin does the body need to help blood clot?
questions.fact: Its letter comes from 'Koagulation', the German word for clotting, used when its discovery was first reported.

questions.q: Who was the first person to walk on the Moon?
questions.fact: Armstrong stepped onto the Moon in July 1969 during the Apollo 11 mission.

questions.q: Who painted the Mona Lisa?
questions.fact: The Mona Lisa hangs in the Louvre museum in Paris.

questions.q: In which country are the pyramids of Giza?
questions.fact: The Great Pyramid is the only one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World still standing.

questions.q: The Great Wall is in which country?
questions.fact: The Great Wall was built and rebuilt over many centuries by different Chinese dynasties.

questions.q: Who was the first President of the United States?
questions.fact: Washington took office as the first president in 1789.

questions.q: In which year did World War II end?
questions.fact: World War II began in 1939 and involved most of the world's nations.

questions.q: In which year did the Titanic sink?
questions.fact: The Titanic sank on its first voyage after hitting an iceberg in the North Atlantic.

questions.q: Which ancient people built the Colosseum?
questions.fact: The Colosseum in Rome could hold tens of thousands of spectators.

questions.q: Who is known as the 'Father of the Nation' in India?
questions.fact: Gandhi led India's independence movement through non-violent protest.

questions.q: In which country did the ancient Olympic Games begin?
questions.fact: The ancient Games were held at Olympia, from 776 BC according to tradition.

questions.q: In which year did Christopher Columbus first reach the Americas?
questions.fact: Columbus was sailing for Spain and hoped to reach Asia.

questions.q: In which year did the Berlin Wall fall?
questions.fact: The wall had divided East and West Berlin since 1961.

questions.q: Which emperor built the Taj Mahal?
questions.fact: Shah Jahan built the Taj Mahal in memory of his wife Mumtaz Mahal.

questions.q: Who was the first woman to win a Nobel Prize?
questions.fact: Marie Curie won Nobel Prizes in both physics and chemistry.

questions.q: Who is credited with inventing the telephone?
questions.fact: Bell was granted a patent for the telephone in 1876.

questions.q: In which year did India gain independence?
questions.fact: India celebrates Independence Day every year on 15 August.

questions.q: Who built Europe's first printing press with movable metal type?
questions.fact: Gutenberg's press, around 1440, helped books and ideas spread across Europe.

questions.q: Which ancient civilisation built Machu Picchu?
questions.fact: Machu Picchu sits high in the Andes mountains of Peru.

questions.q: In which year did World War I begin?
questions.fact: World War I ended with an armistice in November 1918.

questions.q: Cleopatra ruled which ancient kingdom?
questions.fact: Cleopatra was the last active ruler of the Ptolemaic Kingdom of Egypt.

questions.q: The Industrial Revolution began in which country?
questions.fact: It began in the 1700s, as machines and factories started to replace work done by hand.

questions.q: In which year did the French Revolution begin?
questions.fact: The storming of the Bastille on 14 July 1789 is remembered as France's national day.

questions.q: In which year was the US Declaration of Independence adopted?
questions.fact: It was adopted on 4 July, the day the United States celebrates as Independence Day.

questions.q: Which empire did Genghis Khan found?
questions.fact: At its height, the Mongol Empire was the largest land empire in history.

questions.q: Which ancient wonder stood at the harbour of Rhodes?
questions.fact: The Colossus of Rhodes was a giant bronze statue of the sun god Helios.

questions.q: Which Roman town was buried by the eruption of Mount Vesuvius in AD 79?
questions.fact: Excavations began in 1748 and uncovered streets, homes, wall paintings and even loaves of bread turned to charcoal.

questions.q: Orville and Wilbur Wright are famous for pioneering which invention?
questions.fact: Their first powered flight, in North Carolina on 17 December 1903, lasted just 12 seconds.

questions.q: Which pharaoh's largely intact tomb did Howard Carter discover in 1922?
questions.fact: The tomb held more than 5,000 objects, including an inner coffin made of solid gold.

questions.q: In which city is the Forbidden City, the vast palace of China's emperors?
questions.fact: Built between 1406 and 1420, it was the seat of the Ming and Qing emperors for almost 500 years.

questions.q: Which country gave the Statue of Liberty to the United States?
questions.fact: Frédéric Auguste Bartholdi designed it, and Gustave Eiffel engineered its iron framework.

questions.q: Which Paris landmark was built for the World's Fair of 1889?
questions.fact: It was meant to stand for only 20 years, but it was kept because it proved useful for radio signals.

questions.q: What name is given to the ancient trade routes linking China with the Mediterranean?
questions.fact: The name was popularised by the German geographer Ferdinand von Richthofen, who used it in 1877.

questions.q: Who wrote the plays Romeo and Juliet, Hamlet and Macbeth?
questions.fact: Many of his plays were first performed at the Globe, a London theatre built in 1599.

questions.q: Which artist painted the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel?
questions.fact: He worked on it from 1508 to 1512, mostly standing on scaffolding rather than lying on his back.

questions.q: Which Dutch artist painted The Starry Night in 1889?
questions.fact: He painted it while staying at a hospital in Saint-Rémy, in the south of France.

questions.q: Whose diary, written while hiding in Amsterdam in World War II, became world-famous?
questions.fact: She was given the diary, a red-checked autograph book, as a present for her 13th birthday in 1942.

questions.q: Who became South Africa's first Black president in 1994?
questions.fact: He was freed in 1990 after 27 years in prison and shared the 1993 Nobel Peace Prize.

questions.q: Who gave the famous 'I Have a Dream' speech in Washington, D.C., in 1963?
questions.fact: He spoke to a crowd of about 250,000 people from the steps of the Lincoln Memorial.

questions.q: The Magna Carta, sealed by King John in 1215, comes from which country?
questions.fact: It limited the king's power, and three of its clauses are still part of English law today.

questions.q: Which British nurse became known as 'The Lady with the Lamp'?
questions.fact: She nursed soldiers in the Crimean War and in 1860 opened a nursing school in London.

questions.q: Samurai were the warrior class of which country?
questions.fact: The word 'samurai' comes from an old Japanese verb meaning 'to serve'.

questions.q: Who became the first emperor of ancient Rome, in 27 BC?
questions.fact: Known as Octavian before 27 BC, he was Julius Caesar's adopted heir, and August is named after him.

questions.q: Which Indian emperor turned to Buddhism after the Kalinga War?
questions.fact: His lion capital from Sarnath was adopted as the national emblem of India in 1950.

questions.q: The Rosetta Stone was the key to decoding which ancient script?
questions.fact: It repeats one decree in hieroglyphs, Demotic and Greek, which helped Champollion crack the code in 1822.

questions.q: Which explorer led the first voyage from Europe to India by sailing around Africa?
questions.fact: He reached Calicut, on India's south-west coast, in May 1498, opening a sea route for the spice trade.

questions.q: Which people built Tenochtitlan, the island city where Mexico City stands today?
questions.fact: Founded around 1325 on an island in Lake Texcoco, it was linked to the shore by long causeways.

questions.q: Mansa Musa, famous for his vast wealth in gold, ruled which West African empire?
questions.fact: On his pilgrimage to Mecca in 1324, he spent so much gold in Cairo that its value there fell.

questions.q: The Terracotta Army was buried to guard the tomb of which Chinese emperor?
questions.fact: Farmers digging a well near Xi'an found the first of its life-size clay soldiers in 1974.

questions.q: Mohenjo-daro and Harappa were cities of an ancient civilisation named after which river?
questions.fact: Built over 4,000 years ago, its cities had streets laid out in grids and covered drains.

questions.q: Which North African city fought Rome in the three Punic Wars?
questions.fact: Its general Hannibal famously crossed the Alps with war elephants in 218 BC to invade Italy.

questions.q: Simón Bolívar led several South American countries to independence from which power?
questions.fact: Known as 'El Libertador' (The Liberator), he gave his name to the country of Bolivia.

questions.q: Hammurabi, famous for his code of laws, was king of which ancient land?
questions.fact: Around 1750 BC, his laws were carved on a black stone pillar more than 2 metres tall.

questions.q: Angkor Wat, the vast temple in Cambodia, was built by which empire?
questions.fact: Built for King Suryavarman II in the early 1100s, its five towers represent the peaks of Mount Meru.

questions.q: Which city was Japan's imperial capital for over 1,000 years before Tokyo?
questions.fact: It became the capital in 794 under the name Heian-kyō, meaning 'capital of peace'.

questions.q: Who led the first expedition to reach the South Pole, in 1911?
questions.fact: His Norwegian team arrived on 14 December 1911, about five weeks before Robert Scott's party.

questions.q: Which composer wrote his Ninth Symphony while almost completely deaf?
questions.fact: First performed in Vienna in 1824, it ends with a choral setting of the poem 'Ode to Joy'.

questions.q: In which year did Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay reach the top of Mount Everest?
questions.fact: Hillary was a beekeeper from New Zealand, and Tenzing Norgay was a Sherpa mountaineer.

questions.q: The stone city of Great Zimbabwe was built by ancestors of which people?
questions.fact: Its granite walls, some over 10 metres high, were built from fitted blocks without any mortar.

questions.q: Which ancient people carved the city of Petra into the rock of southern Jordan?
questions.fact: Its famous Treasury was carved straight into a pink sandstone cliff about 2,000 years ago.

questions.q: Which Ming dynasty admiral led great treasure fleets as far as East Africa?
questions.fact: He made seven voyages between 1405 and 1433, calling at ports in Southeast Asia, India and Arabia.

questions.q: Persepolis was the grand ceremonial capital of which ancient empire?
questions.fact: Darius the Great began building it around 518 BC, and Alexander the Great burned it in 330 BC.

questions.q: Which city was the Abbasid capital and home of the famous House of Wisdom?
questions.fact: Founded in 762, it was first laid out as a round city, with the caliph's palace at its centre.

questions.q: Which Korean king introduced the Hangul alphabet in the 1440s?
questions.fact: It was designed so that ordinary people, not just scholars, could easily learn to read and write.

questions.q: Who designed the Sydney Opera House, which opened in 1973?
questions.fact: The Danish architect left the project in 1966 and never returned to see his finished building.

questions.q: Which ancient people carved colossal stone heads in Mexico about 3,000 years ago?
questions.fact: Carved from huge basalt boulders, some of the heads stand about 3 metres tall.

questions.q: How many players does a football (soccer) team have on the pitch?
questions.fact: One of the eleven players is the goalkeeper.

questions.q: How many players does a basketball team have on the court?
questions.fact: Basketball was invented in 1891 by James Naismith.

questions.q: How many rings are on the Olympic flag?
questions.fact: The five linked rings stand for the union of the continents.

questions.q: In which sport would you see a slam dunk?
questions.fact: In a slam dunk, a player jumps and pushes the ball down through the hoop.

questions.q: In which game do you say 'checkmate'?
questions.fact: A chessboard has 64 squares.

questions.q: Which sport is played at Wimbledon?
questions.fact: Wimbledon, in London, is the oldest tennis tournament in the world.

questions.q: How many players are in a cricket team?
questions.fact: A cricket match can last anything from about three hours to five days.

questions.q: Which sport is played with a shuttlecock?
questions.fact: A smashed shuttlecock can fly faster than 400 km/h.

questions.q: In which city were the first modern Olympic Games held in 1896?
questions.fact: The modern Games were revived by Pierre de Coubertin of France.

questions.q: In tennis, what does a score of 'love' mean?
questions.fact: Tennis scores go love, 15, 30, 40 and then game.

questions.q: How many holes are played in a standard round of golf?
questions.fact: St Andrews in Scotland is known as the home of golf.

questions.q: What is the official length of a marathon?
questions.fact: The unusual distance comes from the route of the 1908 London Olympics.

questions.q: The Tour de France is a famous race in which sport?
questions.fact: The Tour de France was first held in 1903.

questions.q: What is it called when a footballer scores three goals in one match?
questions.fact: The term 'hat-trick' first came from cricket.

questions.q: Which sport is played with a puck?
questions.fact: Pucks are often frozen before a game so that they bounce less on the ice.

questions.q: How often are the Summer Olympic Games normally held?
questions.fact: The Winter Games are also held every four years, two years apart from the Summer Games.

questions.q: In which country did sumo wrestling originate?
questions.fact: Sumo has ancient roots in Shinto rituals in Japan.

questions.q: How many players does a volleyball team have on the court?
questions.fact: Volleyball was invented in 1895 by William G. Morgan in the United States.

questions.q: In cricket, how many legal balls make up an over?
questions.fact: Each over is bowled by one bowler from one end of the pitch.

questions.q: Which country won the first FIFA World Cup in 1930?
questions.fact: Uruguay also hosted that first World Cup.

questions.q: What shape is a boxing ring?
questions.fact: It is still called a 'ring' because early bare-knuckle fights were held inside a rough circle marked on the ground.

questions.q: Which chess piece moves in an L shape?
questions.fact: A knight always lands on a square of the opposite colour to the one it started on.

questions.q: In cricket, how many runs is a hit that clears the boundary without bouncing?
questions.fact: If the ball bounces before it crosses the boundary, it scores four runs instead.

questions.q: In football (soccer), what colour card does the referee show to send a player off?
questions.fact: Referee Ken Aston got the idea from traffic lights, and the cards were first used at the 1970 World Cup.

questions.q: How long is one lap of the inside lane of a standard outdoor athletics track?
questions.fact: Outer lanes are longer, so in races run in lanes the athletes start at staggered positions.

questions.q: How long is an Olympic-size swimming pool?
questions.fact: A 50-metre pool is known as 'long course', while races in 25-metre pools are called 'short course'.

questions.q: In tennis, what is a score of 40–40 called?
questions.fact: Under standard scoring, a player must then win two points in a row to take the game.

questions.q: Which sport is played on a field known as a 'diamond'?
questions.fact: In professional baseball the bases mark out a square 90 feet (27.4 m) a side, which looks like a diamond from home plate.

questions.q: In which sport do athletes perform on the pommel horse and the balance beam?
questions.fact: The balance beam is 5 metres long but only 10 centimetres wide.

questions.q: In motor racing, what does the black-and-white chequered flag signal?
questions.fact: A yellow flag warns of danger ahead, and drivers must not overtake while it is being waved.

questions.q: How high above the floor is the rim of a basketball hoop?
questions.fact: That is 10 feet, the height of the balcony rail where James Naismith nailed the first peach baskets in 1891.

questions.q: In which sport must a 'raider' keep chanting the game's name in a single breath?
questions.fact: A raider who stops chanting while still in the opponents' half is out. Kabaddi joined the Asian Games in 1990.

questions.q: In which sport can a team be awarded a 'penalty corner'?
questions.fact: In field hockey, a goal only counts if an attacker plays the ball from inside the shooting circle.

questions.q: How long is a cricket pitch, measured between the two sets of stumps?
questions.fact: 22 yards is one 'chain', an old surveyor's unit, equal to about 20.12 metres.

questions.q: Which chess move lets a player move their king and a rook in the same turn?
questions.fact: You can't castle out of check, or once the king or that rook has already moved.

questions.q: Chess developed from chaturanga, an ancient game first played where?
questions.fact: 'Chaturanga' means 'four limbs': the infantry, cavalry, elephants and chariots of an ancient army.

questions.q: Not counting a block, how many hits may an indoor volleyball team use to return the ball?
questions.fact: In beach volleyball a block does count as a hit, so the blocking team has just two more.

questions.q: In rugby union, how many points is a try worth?
questions.fact: In early rugby a try scored nothing: it only earned a 'try' at kicking a goal, hence the name.

questions.q: Which family of board games, where players 'sow' seeds into pits, is played across Africa?
questions.fact: One version, oware from West Africa, uses a board with two rows of six pits and 48 seeds.

questions.q: Which nation's team traditionally leads the parade at the Olympic opening ceremony?
questions.fact: Greece goes first as the home of the ancient Games, and the host nation's team enters last.

questions.q: In the Olympic motto, what does the Latin word 'Citius' mean?
questions.fact: Pierre de Coubertin borrowed the motto 'Citius, Altius, Fortius' from his friend Henri Didon, a Dominican priest.

questions.q: Which city hosted the first Asian Games, in 1951?
questions.fact: The main venue was Delhi's National Stadium, later renamed after the hockey legend Dhyan Chand.

questions.q: How wide is a football (soccer) goal, measured between the posts?
questions.fact: That is 8 yards, and the crossbar sits 8 feet (2.44 metres) above the ground.

questions.q: Badminton is named after Badminton House, a stately home in which country?
questions.fact: British army officers had played a similar game in India, where it was sometimes called 'Poona'.

questions.q: In snooker, how many points is a 'maximum break' worth?
questions.fact: It means potting all 15 reds, each followed by the black, then all six colours in order.

questions.q: Which planet is known as the Red Planet?
questions.fact: Mars looks red because its soil contains a lot of iron oxide, better known as rust.

questions.q: Which is the largest planet in our solar system?
questions.fact: More than 1,300 Earths could fit inside Jupiter.

questions.q: Which planet is closest to the Sun?
questions.fact: A year on Mercury lasts just 88 Earth days.

questions.q: What is the name of our galaxy?
questions.fact: The Milky Way contains hundreds of billions of stars.

questions.q: How many planets are in our solar system?
questions.fact: Pluto was reclassified as a dwarf planet in 2006.

questions.q: What is at the centre of our solar system?
questions.fact: The Sun holds about 99.8% of all the mass in the solar system.

questions.q: Which planet is famous for its bright rings?
questions.fact: Saturn's rings are made mostly of ice, with some dust and rock.

questions.q: What does 'www' stand for in a website address?
questions.fact: The Web is a system of linked pages that runs on the internet, which is the network itself.

questions.q: Which digits does the binary number system use?
questions.fact: Computers store all their information in binary, using just two digits.

questions.q: Roughly how long does Earth take to travel once around the Sun?
questions.fact: The extra quarter of a day each year is why we add a leap day every four years.

questions.q: Which is the hottest planet in our solar system?
questions.fact: Venus is hotter than Mercury because its thick clouds trap heat.

questions.q: Who was the first person to travel into space?
questions.fact: Gagarin orbited Earth once on 12 April 1961.

questions.q: What was the name of the first artificial satellite?
questions.fact: The Soviet Union launched Sputnik 1 in 1957.

questions.q: What does CPU stand for?
questions.fact: The CPU carries out the instructions of computer programs.

questions.q: How many bits are in one byte?
questions.fact: One byte can represent 256 different values.

questions.q: Who invented the World Wide Web?
questions.fact: Berners-Lee created the Web in 1989 while working at CERN in Switzerland.

questions.q: What does RAM stand for?
questions.fact: RAM holds the data a computer is using right away and is cleared when it switches off.

questions.q: Which planet has a giant storm called the Great Red Spot?
questions.fact: The Great Red Spot is a storm wider than the whole Earth.

questions.q: Roughly how long does sunlight take to reach Earth?
questions.fact: Sunlight travels about 150 million km to reach us.

questions.q: Gravity on the Moon is about what fraction of Earth's?
questions.fact: That is why astronauts could bounce across the Moon in their heavy suits.

questions.q: Which planet is the farthest from the Sun?
questions.fact: Neptune takes about 165 Earth years to travel once around the Sun.

questions.q: What does a light-year measure?
questions.fact: A light-year is the distance light travels in a year: about 9.5 trillion km.

questions.q: Who is often called the 'father of the computer'?
questions.fact: In the 1830s Babbage designed the Analytical Engine, a mechanical computer.

questions.q: Who is often described as the first computer programmer?
questions.fact: In 1843 Ada Lovelace published notes on the Analytical Engine that included an algorithm.

questions.q: What does GPS stand for?
questions.fact: GPS works by timing signals from satellites orbiting high above Earth.

questions.q: What is the closest star to Earth?
questions.fact: The next closest star, Proxima Centauri, is about 4.2 light-years away.

questions.q: Which of these units of computer data is the largest?
questions.fact: Each step up is about 1,000 times bigger, so a terabyte is roughly a million megabytes.

questions.q: What is a 'shooting star' actually?
questions.fact: Most are caused by specks of space dust, often no bigger than a grain of sand, burning up in our atmosphere.

questions.q: What is a pixel?
questions.fact: 'Pixel' is short for 'picture element'; a full HD screen has about 2 million of them.

questions.q: What is a named pattern of stars in the night sky called?
questions.fact: Astronomers officially recognise 88 constellations, which together cover the whole sky.

questions.q: The word 'app' is short for what?
questions.fact: The American Dialect Society named 'app' its Word of the Year for 2010.

questions.q: What causes day and night on Earth?
questions.fact: At the equator, Earth's spin carries you along at about 1,670 km/h.

questions.q: In computing, what is a 'bug'?
questions.fact: In 1947 engineers found a real moth trapped in a Harvard computer and taped it into their logbook.

questions.q: During a solar eclipse, what blocks our view of the Sun?
questions.fact: The Sun is about 400 times wider than the Moon but also about 400 times farther away, so both look about the same size.

questions.q: Where does the name of the QWERTY keyboard come from?
questions.fact: Q, W, E, R, T and Y are the first six letters on the top row, a layout designed for typewriters in the 1870s.

questions.q: What is the curved path a planet follows around the Sun called?
questions.fact: In 1609 Johannes Kepler showed that planets' orbits are not perfect circles but slightly stretched ellipses.

questions.q: What is 'phishing' on the internet?
wrong: A way to speed up Wi-Fi
questions.fact: Phishing messages often pretend to come from a bank or a well-known company to win your trust.

questions.q: Roughly how long does the Moon take to go through all its phases?
questions.fact: The word 'month' comes from 'moon'; one full cycle of phases takes about 29.5 days.

questions.q: Solar cells turn sunlight directly into what?
questions.fact: Most solar cells are made of silicon, the same element used to make computer chips.

questions.q: Which space station did the USA, Russia, Europe, Japan and Canada build together?
questions.fact: ISS stands for International Space Station; its first part was launched in 1998.

questions.q: In an email address, which symbol separates the user name from the domain?
questions.fact: Ray Tomlinson chose @ for email in 1971, because it meant 'at' and didn't appear in people's names.

questions.q: Which of these is the space agency of the United States?
questions.fact: NASA was founded in 1958; ESA is Europe's space agency, ISRO is India's and JAXA is Japan's.

questions.q: What is an abacus used for?
questions.fact: In a 1946 contest in Tokyo, an expert using an abacus beat an opponent using an electric calculator.

questions.q: Which planet is tilted so far that it spins on its side?
questions.fact: Its axis is tilted about 98°, so each pole gets around 42 years of sunlight, then 42 years of darkness.

questions.q: A microwave oven heats food mainly by making which molecules move faster?
questions.fact: Engineer Percy Spencer got the idea when radar equipment he was testing melted a sweet in his pocket.

questions.q: Who was the second person to walk on the Moon?
questions.fact: Apollo 11's third astronaut, Michael Collins, stayed in orbit aboard the command module Columbia.

questions.q: Which mathematician helped break the German Enigma code at Bletchley Park?
questions.fact: The Turing test, which asks whether a machine's replies can pass as human, is named after him.

questions.q: Who was the first woman to travel into space?
questions.fact: In 1963 she flew alone aboard Vostok 6 and circled Earth 48 times.

questions.q: What did '.com' in web addresses originally stand for?
questions.fact: It was one of the first domain endings, created in 1985 alongside .org, .net, .edu and .gov.

questions.q: What was the name of the first animal to orbit Earth?
questions.fact: The Soviet dog flew aboard Sputnik 2 in 1957, just a month after Sputnik 1.

questions.q: What do we call a small file that a website stores in your browser to remember you?
questions.fact: Web cookies were invented in 1994 by Lou Montulli, a programmer at Netscape.

questions.q: Which famous comet can be seen from Earth about every 76 years?
questions.fact: Edmond Halley predicted it would return in 1758; it was spotted on Christmas night that year, almost 17 years after his death.

questions.q: In computing, what is an algorithm?
questions.fact: The word comes from al-Khwarizmi, a Persian mathematician who worked in Baghdad in the 800s.

questions.q: Which star is known as the North Star?
questions.fact: It isn't the brightest star, but it lies almost directly above Earth's North Pole, so it barely moves.

questions.q: What does a computer firewall do?
questions.fact: It's named after the fireproof walls in buildings that stop a fire from spreading.

questions.q: What causes Earth's seasons?
questions.fact: Earth is actually closest to the Sun in early January, during the northern winter.

questions.q: Morse code was first created for use with which invention?
questions.fact: In Morse code, the distress signal SOS is three dots, three dashes and three dots.

questions.q: India's Mangalyaan probe, launched in 2013, went into orbit around which planet?
questions.fact: In 2014 it made India the first country to reach Mars orbit on its first attempt.

questions.q: On a network, what is an IP address mainly used for?
questions.fact: IP stands for Internet Protocol; the older IPv4 system has room for about 4.3 billion addresses.

questions.q: Which is the nearest major galaxy to our own Milky Way?
questions.fact: Its light takes about 2.5 million years to reach us, yet on a dark night it can be seen without a telescope.

questions.q: What does LED stand for?
questions.fact: Bright blue LEDs took decades to develop; their inventors won the 2014 Nobel Prize in Physics.

questions.q: Which spacecraft carried Philae, the first probe to soft-land on a comet?
questions.fact: Rosetta orbited comet 67P for about two years, then ended its mission in 2016 by touching down on the comet itself.

questions.q: What was the name of the early computer network that grew into the internet?
questions.fact: Its first message, in 1969, was meant to be 'LOGIN', but the system crashed after 'LO'.

questions.q: In 2019, China's Chang'e 4 made the first soft landing on which part of the Moon?
questions.fact: Because the far side never faces Earth, a relay satellite called Queqiao passed its signals home.

questions.q: China's 'Four Great Inventions' are the compass, gunpowder, printing and what?
questions.fact: Tradition credits Cai Lun, a Han dynasty court official, with improving papermaking around 105 CE.

questions.q: Japan's Hayabusa was the first spacecraft to bring back samples from what?
questions.fact: In 2010 it brought home tiny grains from asteroid Itokawa; 'Hayabusa' is Japanese for peregrine falcon.

questions.q: What does 'QR' stand for in QR code?
questions.fact: QR codes were invented in Japan in 1994 to track car parts in factories.

questions.q: Who made the first ever spacewalk, in 1965?
questions.fact: His spacesuit puffed up in the vacuum, and he had to let air out of it to squeeze back inside.

questions.q: The word 'robot' comes from a Czech word meaning what?
questions.fact: The word was introduced in Karel Čapek's 1920 play R.U.R., about artificial factory workers.

questions.q: What is a black hole's boundary, past which nothing can escape, called?
questions.fact: In 2019 astronomers revealed the first image of a black hole's shadow, in the galaxy M87.
